3C. WAIVE FURTHER READING AND ADOPT AN OMNIBUS ORDINANCE

  The City Council waived second reading and adopted ordinance at the March 3,
  2021 meeting. Through inadvertence, however, Exhibits A and B to the ordinance
  were not included with the staff report. In an abundance of caution, therefore, the
  City Clerk’s office asks that the City Council again adopt the ordinance with all
  exhibits.

  Other than the inclusion of the attached exhibits there are no other changes from
  the first reading that occurred on February 1, 2021.

  The original staff report (from February 17, 2021) is attached to the staff report for
  reference. Second reading and adoption of this Ordinance is recommended. If
  adopted, the Ordinance will take effect in 30 days.

  The proposed amendments are to further enact and make permanent procedural
  changes that further implement and carry out the city’s goals and policies
  established by the Monterey Park Business Recovery Program (“BRP”). As part of
  the BRP, various elements of the Monterey Park Municipal Code (“MPMC”),
  specifically Title 21 as it relates to variances, conditional use permits, minor
  modifications, and administrative use permits warranted further refinement to
  establish consistency amongst the aforementioned sections including, without
  limitation, processing procedures, public hearing requirements, standards and
  expirations.

  Additionally, the ordinance would repeal regulations governing fortunetelling within
  the MPMC. A series of court cases over the past decade made it plain that the
  practice of fortunetelling constitutes a First Amendment activity as both an exercise
  of religion and free speech. Most recently, an individual seeking to open a
  fortunetelling business in Monterey Park threatened litigation in December 2020.
  The matter was resolved, in part, by the City agreeing to propose amendments to
  the MPMC to reflect current federal and California law governing fortunetelling
  activities. These changes were vetted, among other City departments, with the
  Monterey Park Police Department. There were no objections to the changes.

  Action Taken: The City Council waived the second reading and adopted
  Ordinance No. 2203 on Consent Calendar.

5A. CITY COUNCIL DISTRICTING – CENSUS DATA UPDATE

  In accordance with the Fair And Inclusive Redistricting for Municipalities And
  Political Subdivisions (FAIR MAPS) Act (Elections Code § 21600-21609), following
  each decennial federal census, the City Council must adopt a map showing the
  district boundaries city council offices so that the districts will be substantially equal
  in population. Certain requirements must be met before the City Council adopts the
  final district voting map. This includes holding at least four public hearings, good
  faith effort in engaging in community involvement, maintaining a dedicated
  webpage for providing redistricting information, and providing translated materials
  and live translation upon request.

  Recent legislation changed the redistricting process. This report is intended to give
  the City Council an overview of the redistricting process and the timeline affecting
  the submittal of the new district map. The combination of the when the next
  regularly scheduled election date and when the City receives the census data will
  determine the deadline for submitting the new City Council district boundary map.

  The U.S. Census Bureau announced on February 12, 2021 that the 2020 Census
  redistricting data will be released by September 30, 2021. The Statewide Database
  will require an additional 30 days to adjust the datasets for redistricts. In
  accordance with Elections Code § 21602, the boundaries of council districts must
  be adopted not later than 174 days before the City’s next regular municipal
  election. The City Council has not yet decided whether that election will be held in
  June 2022 or November 2022. The Los Angeles County Registrar Recorder’s
  office’s deadline for submittal of new district map is December 9, 2021 for the June
  7, 2022 election and May 12, 2022 for the November 8, 2022 election.

May 12-18—to honor and remember those law enforcement officers who made the
ultimate sacrifice, as well as the family members, friends, and fellow officers they left
behind.

RECOMMENDATION:

  1. Adopting a resolution identifying a street maintenance project to be included in the
  FY 2021-22 budget and funded with Road Maintenance and Rehabilitation Act
  (RMRA) funds, in a form approved by the City Attorney; and
  2. Take such additional, related action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
Senate Bill 1 (SB 1), the Road Repair and Accountability Act of 2017 addresses the
significant multi-modal transportation funding shortfall statewide. As of November 2017,
portions of SB 1 revenues are deposited into a Road Maintenance and Rehabilitation
Account (RMRA) and made available to eligible cities and counties, which must comply
with RMRA funding requirements as determined by the California Transportation
Commission (CTC).

RMRA funds made available for the Local Streets and Roads Funding Program are
prioritized for expenditure on basic road maintenance and rehabilitation projects, and on
critical safety projects. The CTC provided a number of example projects and uses for
RMRA funding that include, but are not limited to, the following: Road Maintenance and
Rehabilitation, Safety Projects, Railroad Grade Separations, Complete Streets
Components (including active transportation purposes, pedestrian and bicycle safety
projects, transit facilities, and drainage and stormwater capture projects in conjunction
with any other allowable project), and Traffic Control Devices.

BACKGROUND:
The most recent State estimates for FY 2021-22 project Monterey Park will receive
$1,103,381 in RMRA funds. In order to be eligible to receive these funds, normally
agencies must submit a proposed project list to the CTC by May 1, 2021, along with
budget support documentation including the council meeting minutes and/or resolution of
the City Council committing to the project list. This year, project lists are due July 1, 2021.

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:

  1. Introducing and waiving first reading of an Ordinance amending Chapter 9.90 of
  the Monterey Park Municipal Code in its entirety to regulate graffiti in conformance
  with California law; or
  2. Taking such additional, related action that may be desirable.

CEQA (California Environmental Quality Act):

Adoption of this Resolution is exempt from the California Environmental Quality Act
(“CEQA”) under CEQA Guidelines § 15061(b)(3) because it can be seen with certainty
that there is no possibility that the Ordinance may have a significant effect on the
environment.

BACKGROUND:

Within the City, the effect of graffiti in the form of spray paint, tagging with indelible ink,
etching surfaces, and stickers on public and private property have proven to be a blight,
particularly in certain areas. Published sociological studies and the experience of law
enforcement indicate a correlation between the presence of graffiti and increased
instances of littering, theft and other crimes in those same neighborhoods.

Chapter 9.90 of the Monterey Park Municipal Code (“MPMC”), which regulates graffiti,
has not been updated or amended since 1993. Since that time, there have been changes
to state vandalism laws, enforcement of such laws by the Los Angeles District Attorney,
and changes in circumstances within the City.

While acts of vandalism are a crime under state law (see Penal Code § 594, et seq.), the
California Constitution and Penal Code empowers the City to enact and enforce
ordinances regulating conditions that may be public nuisances or health hazards, or that

  Page 95 of 126

promote social, economic, or aesthetic considerations. Government Code § 38771
permits general law cities to identify public nuisances by ordinance.

This Ordinance would revise Chapter 9.90 of the MPMC to designate acts related to
graffiti as public nuisances and unlawful. It is specifically intended to be responsive to
the many different ways in which graffiti is currently being applied, how graffiti
implements are made available to violators, to prohibit the possession of implements
intended to be used for graffiti, and provide a means of enforcement through the
Monterey Park Police Department and City Attorney’s office by making these violations
misdemeanors.

In December 2020, Los Angeles County District Attorney George Gascon announced
he would no longer prosecute a range of “low level” misdemeanor offenses. This
includes quality-of-life crimes and most municipal code offenses. The Monterey
Park Police Department and City Attorney’s Office are coordinating efforts to
begin citing and criminally prosecuting applicable MPMC violations, including graffiti
offenses.

In addition to criminal enforcement efforts, this Ordinance also allows for civil
enforcement for the removal of graffiti as public nuisances and for the City to recoup
costs related to abatement of such nuisances, including treble damages for repeat
offenders.

This Ordinance further authorizes the use of rewards for information leading to
the apprehension and conviction of any person who commits a graffiti offense on any
public or private property within the city.

FISCAL IMPACT:

Adopting the Ordinance itself will have a nominal fiscal impact in requiring the Assistant
City Attorney or deputy city attorney to appear in court up to one day per month to
prosecute graffiti offenses along with other misdemeanor MPMC violations. The City will
receive offsetting revenue from fines paid by persons prosecuted. It is difficult to predict
exactly how much the City will receive from such fines. Civil enforcement as a public
nuisance will also have a nominal fiscal impact, as this Ordinance specifically provides
for recouping City costs associated with abatement efforts.

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:

  1. Adopting a Resolution establishing a bail schedule for misdemeanor and infraction
  violations of the Monterey Park Municipal Code; or
  2. Taking such additional, related action that may be desirable.

CEQA (California Environmental Quality Act):

Adoption of this Resolution is exempt from the California Environmental Quality Act
(“CEQA”) under CEQA Guidelines § 15061(b)(3) because it can be seen with certainty
that there is no possibility that the Resolution may have a significant effect on the
environment.

BACKGROUND:

In December 2020, Los Angeles County District Attorney George Gascon announced he
would no longer prosecute a range of “low level” misdemeanor offenses. This includes
quality-of-life crimes, such as trespass, disturbing the peace, criminal threats, resisting
arrest, loitering, and public intoxication. District Attorney Gascon’s non-prosecution
directives also apply to any violation “falling within the spirit” of this policy, which
necessarily includes violations of the Monterey Park Municipal Code (“MPMC”).

Most violations of the MPMC constitute a misdemeanor that may be punished by a $1000
fine, six months in jail, or both (MPMC § 4.10.010). This reflects California law
(Government Code § 36900 and Penal Code § 802).

The result of District Attorney Gascon’s non-prosecution policy has been to severely
hamper the ability of the Monterey Park Police Department to protect and serve the
residents of this City. To address this policy, the Police Department seeks to use
violations of the Monterey Park Municipal Code (“MPMC”), when applicable, to encourage
compliance with the law, and have MPMC violations prosecuted by the City Attorney’s

office in lieu of the District Attorney. Enforcement of the MPMC includes: disturbing the
peace, graffiti, unruly gatherings, damage to public property, weapon possession, sale
of narcotics paraphernalia, unpermitted cannabis dispensaries, and a variety of
other activities that directly affect the peaceful enjoyment of this City.

A bail schedule establishes the amount a person booked into jail must post for release
as security to ensure their appearance at a future court date. Additionally, for the
Court to accept misdemeanor or infraction violations of the MPMC for criminal
prosecution, a bail amount must be established for each MPMC section the City wishes
the court to hear.

The City does not have a current bail schedule submitted to the Superior Court, and
criminal violations of the MPMC are therefore not being accepted for criminal
prosecution. Submitting this bail schedule will provide the City the opportunity to
more effectively address many quality-of-life crimes that the District Attorney would
otherwise decline to accept for prosecution.

If adopted, the draft Resolution would not only establish a bail schedule to allow for the
criminal prosecution of violations of the MPMC, but the Superior Court will also use the
bail schedule as a guide for imposing fine amounts when a violator is found guilty. For
infraction violations, the MPMC establishes a default fine schedule of $100/$200/
$500, which is followed in the proposed bail schedule.1 $500 is the default bail
amount for misdemeanor municipal code violations throughout the County, which is
also used in this Bail Schedule. The court can still impose fines up $1,000 per
misdemeanor violation.

Please note that this bail schedule is different than fine amounts established
for administrative citations. Any updates to the administrative fine schedule will be
addressed in a future City Council meeting.

FISCAL IMPACT:

Adopting the Resolution itself will have a nominal fiscal impact in requiring the Assistant
City Attorney or deputy city attorney to appear in court up to one day per month to
prosecute misdemeanor MPMC violations. The City will receive offsetting revenue from
fines paid by persons prosecuted. It is difficult to predict exactly how much the City will
receive from such fines.

  A. On May 6, 1882, President Chester Arthur signed the Chinese Exclusion Act,

  B. The Chinese Exclusion Act, based on racial hostility against the Chinese, was
  characterized as “unassimilable, vile heathens” and were blamed for lowering
  wages, taking away jobs, draining the economy, and endangering the American
  way of life.

  C. The Chinese Exclusion Act, which was renewed in 1892, 1902, and made
  permanent in 1904, prevented Chinese laborers from entering the U.S. and
  denied Chinese a pathway to citizenship for more than 60 years.

  D. Chinese and Chinese Americans in the United States have suffered every
  moment, every action, every offense, and every heartbreak, as triggered and
  scripted by that Act.

  E. The U.S. Senate in 2011 and the U.S. House of Representatives in 2012
  unanimously condemned in Resolutions the Chinese Exclusion Laws and
  “affirmed Congress” commitment to preserving the civil rights and constitutional
  protections for all people.

  F. America is greater and more prosperous because we practice the ideals of
  inclusion, embracing everyone regardless of race, color, national original,
  religion, or gender.

  G. Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders strengthen our economy as
  entrepreneurs, business owners, and employees who initiate and expand
  opportunities for their families, communities, and country. Their languages, art,
  cuisine, and other cultural elements have enriched the American experience.
  Many have fearlessly responded to the call of duty to defend our freedom as
  members of our Armed Forces.

  H. Approximately 21 million residents of the United States identify themselves as
